problems.description: Measured convention score 0.70 (9 violations) is dominated by pre-existing issues in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py); the only touched-file flags are 'Classes should use PascalCase' on app.py and test_app.py, which this diff does not introduce — no classes are added in the +11 functions.

init_db() now runs as a module-level side effect at import time; since the test fixture monkeypatches DATABASE only after import, the module-level call also creates the default tasks.db in the working directory during test runs (the fixture then re-inits against tmp_path, making the module-level call partially redundant).

strengths: Removes dead code (legacy date helper, unused _notify_admin stub, fetch_task alias) — net -19 lines
Fixes the new-task default status bug ('done' → 'pending'), correcting the DB default
Switches to timezone-aware UTC timestamps via a single _now() helper
Adds a comprehensive pytest suite with tmp_path/monkeypatch DB isolation covering create/list/get/update and 400/404 error paths
Refactor stays within existing Flask patterns and module structure
commit_reviews.summary: Clean greenfield-baseline commit that removes dead code, fixes the new-task status semantics, and adds a solid test suite — the measured 0.70 convention score is driven mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files, not by this diff.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded dev default when the env var is unset; anyone can forge tokens if the app is deployed without SECRET_KEY configured. Acceptable for a story app, but should fail closed in production.
Schema migration via PRAGMA table_info introspection inside init_db is heavier than the seed's plain CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS; fine at tier-1 scale, but the pattern won't scale to real migrations.
PRAGMA table_info uses an unparameterizable string identifier; safe here since the table name is a constant, but worth noting it must never accept user input.

strengths: All SQL is parameterized — no injection surface introduced
Migration guard (ALTER TABLE only when owner_id is absent) preserves pre-existing task data
Row-level authorization scoped into WHERE clauses on read/update, not just authentication
Consistent JSON error shape with correct status codes (400/401/409/201)
Passwords hashed with werkzeug, never stored in plaintext
Idiomatic Flask: token_required decorator with @wraps, g.current_user, per-route auth wiring
Faithfully follows the seed's conventions — get_db()/with-conn pattern, dict(row) conversion, _now(), banner comments, UPPER_CASE constants, type hints on public signatures
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-scoped feature addition that implements JWT auth and per-user task ownership while closely mirroring the seed's structure and conventions; the measured convention score of 0.70 reflects pre-existing violations in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) — the only app.py violation flagged (PascalCase classes) cannot apply since this diff adds zero classes — so the commit's own convention adherence is higher than the mechanical score.

problems.description: Measured convention score 0.70 with 9 violations. New modules carry most: celery_config.py (broker_url, result_backend, accept_content, task_serializer, timezone, task_routes lowercase) and tasks.py (celery_app, logger) violate module-level UPPER_CASE. Note: Celery's documented config_from_object pattern uses lowercase settings, so some of these are framework-idiomatic tension with the repo linter rather than outright errors.
Measured violations list repositories.py (module-level UPPER_CASE), but that file is untouched by this diff — a pre-existing flag, not introduced here.

The test_app.py 'Classes should use PascalCase' flag appears to target _FakeEmailTask, which already is PascalCase (leading underscore aside) — a possible analyzer false positive worth noting against the 0.70 score.

Notification-trigger logic is inlined in the edit_task route handler (app.py:270-277) rather than extracted into a service/domain layer; acceptable at this app size but couples business rule to transport.
user_email is fabricated as f"{g.current_user['username']}@example.com" — hardcoded fake domain instead of a real user email field; works for the mock but is data-quality debt.
Redis broker/result URLs hardcoded to localhost:6379/0 in celery_config.py with no env override; fine for the story sandbox but not portable.
tasks.py emits both logger.info and print for the same notification — redundant output channels.

Tests mock send_notification_email entirely (monkeypatched fake), so the Celery task body itself is never executed; acceptable since it is a log/print stub, but the 'async flow verified' claim rests on the mock.

strengths: Correct async pattern: send_notification_email.delay(...) enqueues and returns immediately, keeping the request path non-blocking.
Transition detection (old_task status check before update) prevents duplicate emails when a task is re-marked completed.
Dedicated 'emails' queue via task_routes gives clean separation for the async consumer; task name matches the routing key exactly.
Clean Celery application layout: separate tasks.py (app) + celery_config.py (config), matching Celery's documented structure.
Strong test suite — 5 cases cover the transition trigger, non-completed statuses, title-only updates, idempotency, and the 404 path, with a monkeypatch fake that avoids needing Redis in unit tests.
Reuses existing data-layer functions (get_task, update_task) rather than re-implementing persistence.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured Celery async integration with strong transition-detection logic and thorough tests; the only real deductions are the measured convention score (0.70, partly Celery-idiomatic lowercase config) and minor maintainability nits like the fabricated email domain and hardcoded Redis URL.

problems.description: repositories.py's _connection() lazily imports app to call app.get_db(), creating a circular module dependency (app imports repositories, repositories imports app) and coupling the data layer to the Flask app module rather than injecting a connection factory — works only in this single-module layout and would break under an app-factory pattern.

The refactor moves ~200 lines of SQL into a brand-new repository layer (+1 file, no test file added/changed) with no direct unit tests; only the pre-existing behavior-preserving integration suite covers it indirectly.

Measured convention score 0.70 (9 violations) is inflated by pre-existing violations in files this diff does not touch (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py, and the app.py 'Classes should use PascalCase' flag, which is an analyzer heuristic on a routes-only file); the commit's own new code contributes only the repositories.py module-constant flag.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: all SQLite access moved out of app.py into a cohesive repository layer, shrinking the route module by ~112 lines with net code reduction
BaseRepository(ABC) genuinely enforces the CRUD contract via abstractmethods (unlike many variants that declare ABC without abstract methods), and concrete repos keep typed signatures

Behavior-preserving refactor — route handlers delegate to repository methods with identical semantics and owner_id scoping preserved; old model functions removed outright with no dead wrappers or parallel access paths
Follows the established get_db()/section-banner Flask idioms and the story's Repository-pattern requirement, consistent with the minimal single-app architecture
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive, behavior-preserving repository-layer refactor that properly isolates persistence and enforces the CRUD contract via a real ABC, dragged by a circular-import smell in _connection() and a measured 0.70 convention score that is mostly pre-existing noise in untouched files (only the repositories.py constant-case flag is attributable to this commit).

problems.description: limiter.init_app(app) runs at module import in app.py and is re-invoked in the test fixture after swapping RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI. Double init_app is tolerated today but is fragile coupling between prod and test wiring; a create_app factory would be cleaner.
_rate_limit_key decodes the JWT on every request even though @token_required already validates it on authenticated routes — a redundant HS256 decode per request.

The /tasks response shape changes from a bare list to a paginated envelope {"data", "next_cursor", "total"} — a breaking API contract change for any existing consumers (acceptable mid-story, but worth an explicit callout).
Adds flask-limiter and defaults RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI to redis://localhost:6379/0; verify the dependency lands in requirements and note the limiter fails requests if Redis is unavailable.

strengths: Pagination is correctly layered in the repository (list_for_owner_paginated) following the existing list_for_owner pattern, using keyset/cursor (id < cursor) instead of OFFSET and clamping limit to 1..100.
Rate limiting is security-positive and user-aware: authenticated requests bucket by JWT user_id, unauthenticated (auth endpoints) fall back to client IP, with a proper 429 handler.
Strong test coverage for the new behavior: envelope shape, default limit of 20, full cursor walk across three pages, and the 100 cap.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-architected session that adds user-aware rate limiting and keyset pagination cleanly inside the existing repository/route/test patterns — the measured 0.70 convention score is dragged by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py), not by this diff's snake_case/typed/docstringed new code.

compounding_issues: Retrofitted ownership: session 2 added a nullable owner_id via ALTER TABLE, so tasks created in the pre-auth seed (session 1) have NULL owner_id and silently disappear from all users' filtered queries — handled non-destructively but leaves orphaned rows.
app.py grew toward ~300 lines after session 3 (JWT + Celery + notification trigger all in one file); session 4's repository extraction was a required cleanup rather than optional polish.
Git hygiene: todos.db and __pycache__ .pyc files are committed alongside source (session 1 onward), polluting the history with derived/binary artifacts.

Session 5's rate-limit key decodes the JWT on every request purely for bucketing, and the Celery/RateLimiter both default to localhost Redis — deployment-dependent coupling that the tests paper over with memory:// and mocks.
key_decisions: Single-file Flask + sqlite3 app with deliberately clean seams (models/routes/error handling separated) as the seed, giving later sessions a safe base to extend.
JWT auth with per-user task ownership: owner_id column added via a non-destructive PRAGMA-driven ALTER TABLE migration, plus a token_required decorator enforcing user isolation at the route level.

Async email notifications via Celery + Redis with a dedicated 'emails' task queue, firing only on the pending->completed transition (explicit guards prevent retrigger on already-completed tasks and on title-only updates).

Repository pattern refactor (BaseRepository ABC + Task/User repositories) pulling all raw SQL out of the routes, with a lazy `import app` in _connection() that preserves the test fixture's monkeypatch seam.

Cross-cutting session built on the data layer: cursor-based pagination inside the repository (limit+1 lookahead, {data, next_cursor, total} envelope) plus Flask-Limiter with Redis storage keyed by JWT user_id.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions. It started as a minimal 135-line single-file CRUD API with 9 tests and evolved through auth (user isolation), async integration (Celery notifications with correct edge-case semantics), and a structural refactor that pulled the data layer into typed repositories — the refactor was the strongest signal, since it shrank app.py by ~40% while keeping all 25 existing tests green with zero regressions. Session 5 finished with production-grade cross-cutting concerns: per-user rate limiting, validated cursor pagination with capped limits, and a 33-test suite (test/code ratio 0.68) that passed cleanly on re-run. Effort tracked difficulty — session 5 consumed 4.6x the tokens of session 1 — but every session landed green with confidence 1.0, and each session's additions were built on the seams laid down by the one before it.
